result: A double-sided microscope system was developed by mounting an upright and inverted fluorescent microscope with precisely aligned 20x objectives, using a high-power LED for excitation, with the top objective operating in epifluorescence mode and functioning as a condenser for the bottom objective operating in transfluorescence mode. The system was assembled from conventional optical parts and included technical modifications to suppress vibration noise.
evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C24-C31, C71, C119-C120, and C130-C131 provide comprehensive technical details about the microscope construction, optical configuration, and hardware specifications. The design is well-documented with specific component details, alignment procedures, and technical justifications (e.g., high NA preventing illumination inhomogeneities in C30). The system represents a novel technical achievement for simultaneous dual-plane imaging.

result: The double-sided microscope enabled recording from all cell bodies of a leech ganglion regardless of their location and allowed direct analysis of functional relationships between neurons on opposite surfaces for the first time, though not all neurons could be simultaneously in sharp focus due to surface curvature.
evaluation: Claims C3, C4, and C81 establish the key capability of the system. The claim of 'first time' analysis (C4) is explicitly stated and represents a major advance. The limitation regarding focus (C81) is appropriately acknowledged. These claims are supported by the experimental demonstrations throughout the manuscript showing simultaneous recording from both ganglion surfaces.

result: The VF2.1(OMe).H voltage-sensitive dye achieved a sensitivity of 2.7 ± 0.3% per 100 mV at resting potential in leech ganglia and faithfully detected various membrane potential changes including action potentials, synaptic potentials, and rhythmic oscillations. The system could capture discrete unitary EPSPs (2-4 mV) as optical signals (0.02-0.04% ΔF/F) and reconstructed relatively large, slow action potentials in several cell types. Photon noise was comparable between top and bottom images.
evaluation: Claims C31-C33, C88, and C109 provide quantitative characterization of the dye's performance with specific measurements and error estimates. The sensitivity measurement (C31) is based on five ganglia from two animals with appropriate statistical reporting. The detection of various signal types (C32) is demonstrated in Figure 1d. The photon noise comparison (C33) shows no substantial difference between imaging planes, validating the optical design.

result: Double-sided imaging produced results indistinguishable from conventional single-sided imaging in terms of coherence maps, signal amplitudes, noise levels, and coherence between bilateral homologues, indicating no compromise in imaging quality.
evaluation: Claims C39-C43 provide critical validation that the double-sided approach does not sacrifice imaging quality. The comparison is supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1 with statistical analysis (ANOVA, p>0.05 for all comparisons). This addresses a key concern about whether the novel optical configuration introduces artifacts or reduces signal quality. The inference in C43 is well-justified by the quantitative comparisons in C40-C42.

result: During fictive swimming induced by DP nerve stimulation, rhythmic activity was readily observed, and the system confirmed oscillatory behavior of neurons previously studied with earlier-generation dyes while also detecting weaker oscillations in many other neurons on both sides of the ganglion.
evaluation: Claims C34-C38 describe the swimming behavior experiments with appropriate methodological details (C34) and results. The confirmation of previously known patterns (C37) validates the technique, while detection of additional neurons (C38) demonstrates enhanced sensitivity. The use of DI-1 as a phase reference (C36) is well-established. Results are supported by Figure 2 and comparison to prior work (Briggman and Kristan, 2006).

result: In local bending experiments, stimulation of PV cells reliably evoked action potentials, and on average 113±11 ventral and 129±6 dorsal cells could be mapped to identified neurons across eight experiments. Among these, 28% of ventral and 36% of dorsal cells encoded stimulus identity with >75% prediction success during the first 0.5s of stimulation, including LBIs, motor neurons, AP cells, Leydig cells, and other provisionally identified neurons. Control period prediction was at chance level (50.9±1.3%).
evaluation: Claims C48-C57 provide comprehensive quantitative results from the local bending experiments with appropriate sample sizes (N=8), statistical measures (mean±SD), and controls. The prediction success analysis (C52-C53) uses a rigorous leave-one-out cross-validation approach. The control comparison (C56) demonstrates specificity. The identification of specific cell types (C54, C57) is supported by Figure 3 and established anatomical knowledge. The methodology for calculating prediction success is detailed in Materials and Methods.

result: All three behaviors (local bending, swimming, crawling) could be induced in each of six animals. On average, 126±11 ventral and 121±10 dorsal cells could be assigned to identified neurons. Approximately 10% of cells were involved in all three behaviors, 33% in two behaviors, 42% in a single behavior, 9% in none, and 6% could not be assessed due to lack of samples.
evaluation: Claims C58-C65 present the multi-behavior analysis with clear quantitative results and appropriate sample size (N=6). The percentages sum to 100% (accounting for the 6% unassigned), indicating comprehensive accounting. The results are supported by Figure 4j and Videos 1-4. The acknowledgment of limitations (C65) demonstrates scientific rigor. The ability to induce all three behaviors in each animal (C58) is important for within-subject comparisons.

result: Clustering analysis revealed that during crawling and especially local bending, most clusters were largely confined to one side of the ganglion, whereas during swimming clusters more commonly spanned both sides, indicating that swimming involves correlated activity among cells on both surfaces while local bending largely does not.
evaluation: Claims C66-C68 describe a novel finding enabled by double-sided imaging. The clustering analysis methodology is described in Materials and Methods, and results are quantified with an integration coefficient (Figure 5c) showing statistically significant differences between behaviors (ANOVA, F(2,15)=63.4, p<10⁻⁷). The inference in C68 is well-supported by the quantitative data in C66-C67. This represents a previously unappreciated difference between behaviors that could only be observed with simultaneous dual-surface imaging.

result: Many neurons beyond previously reported LBIs and motor neurons discriminated between left and right stimuli in local bending. Additionally, 43% of identifiable neurons were involved in at least two of three behaviors tested, indicating that neural circuits for these behaviors share many components while generating unique motor patterns.
evaluation: Claims C92, C95, and C96 present key biological findings. C92 extends previous knowledge (Lockery and Kristan, 1990) by identifying additional discriminating neurons. C95 provides a specific quantitative result, and C96 draws a reasonable inference about circuit overlap. These findings are supported by the comprehensive mapping data (Figures 3-4) and represent important insights into how the leech nervous system organizes behavioral control. The inference in C96 is justified by the quantitative overlap data.

result: Double-sided imaging revealed a previously unappreciated difference between swimming and local bending in terms of cell assembly distribution across ganglion surfaces, though the functional significance of this difference remains unknown.
evaluation: Claims C102 and C103 identify a novel finding while appropriately acknowledging uncertainty about its functional significance. C102 is supported by the clustering analysis (Figure 5) and represents a discovery only possible with double-sided imaging. C103 appropriately identifies this as an open question for future research. The claim of 'previously unappreciated' is justified as this spatial organization could not be observed with single-sided imaging.

result: The percentage of circuit components shared between swimming and crawling differed from previous work, with fewer cells identified as involved in crawling (56 vs. 188 in Briggman and Kristan 2006). This difference is attributed to double-sided desheathing making long crawling episodes rare, resulting in shorter episodes (3-4 cycles) and weaker coherence signals, combined with shorter imaging duration (50s vs. 60s) to achieve higher frame rate.
evaluation: Claims C97-C101 acknowledge a discrepancy with prior work and provide plausible explanations. The comparison to Briggman and Kristan (2006) is explicit and quantitative (C98). The explanations (C99-C101) are reasonable given the methodological differences required for double-sided imaging. The authors appropriately discuss this limitation rather than ignoring the discrepancy. However, this does indicate that the double-sided preparation may have some constraints on certain behaviors.

result: The CCD camera frame rate (50 Hz for local bending/swimming, 20 Hz for crawling) restricted imaging of brief action potentials, with long-lasting potentials easy to detect but millisecond-order spikes difficult to detect at 50 Hz. Higher frame rates (200 Hz) would enable sufficient reconstruction of brief spikes, though the system successfully reconstructed relatively large, slow action potentials in several cell types.
evaluation: Claims C104-C109 provide an honest assessment of system limitations and capabilities. The frame rate specifications (C105-C106) are clearly stated. The limitation for brief spikes (C107) is acknowledged, with reference to prior work (C108) showing that higher frame rates would address this. The successful detection of slower spikes (C109) demonstrates that the system is still useful for many applications. This represents appropriate scientific transparency about technical limitations.

result: The VoltageFluor dye has negligible delay (nanosecond to microsecond) compared to FRET-based dyes (millisecond to second), eliminating the need for phase delay adjustment. This faster response likely explains why AE cells showing swim-related oscillation were detected in this study but not in previous work using slower dyes at lower frame rates, and enabled higher coherence detection in these neurons.
evaluation: Claims C110-C115 compare the current dye to previous technology with appropriate citations (Miller et al., 2012; Briggman and Kristan, 2006). The speed comparison (C111) is quantitative and well-documented. The inference about why AE cells were detected (C114) is reasonable given the methodological differences. The improved coherence (C115) is supported by the data in Figure 2a. This demonstrates a clear advantage of the new dye over previous approaches.

result: Data processing included custom motion correction algorithms, bleaching correction using locally fitted cubic polynomials, subtraction of global fluctuations, and semi-automated cell mapping using a custom user interface to establish correspondence between fluorescent images and canonical neuron maps.
evaluation: Claims C122-C125 describe essential data processing steps with appropriate citations (Wagenaar and Potter, 2002; Lippert et al., 2007). The motion correction (C122) is detailed in Figure 1—figure supplement 2. The cell mapping procedure (C125) is illustrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 1. These methods are critical for obtaining reliable results from VSD imaging and are appropriately documented. The semi-automated approach balances efficiency with expert validation.

result: Ca2+ imaging is limited to intracellular events associated with Ca2+ concentration changes, measuring neither subthreshold depolarizing nor hyperpolarizing synaptic events, making it difficult to observe synaptic integration. In contrast, VSDs can detect both action potentials and subthreshold excitatory and inhibitory synaptic potentials.
evaluation: Claims C5-C8 present established knowledge about the limitations of Ca2+ imaging and advantages of VSDs. These are well-known facts in the field and provide important context for why VSD imaging was chosen. The claims accurately characterize the capabilities and limitations of each technique. This background information is essential for understanding the motivation for the study.

result: The leech CNS consists of a ventral nerve cord connecting a head brain, 21 nearly identical segmental ganglia, and a tail brain. Each segmental ganglion contains approximately 400 identifiable neurons (148 with published functional descriptions), mostly as bilateral pairs, arranged in a well-preserved geometry in a single spherical shell surrounding a central neuropil. The neurons wrap around both dorsal and ventral sides, so at best half can be simultaneously imaged with conventional microscopy.
evaluation: Claims C12-C16 and C77-C80 provide essential anatomical background about the leech nervous system with appropriate citations (Pipkin et al., 2016; Kristan et al., 2005). These are well-established facts that explain why the leech is a suitable model system and why double-sided imaging is necessary. The inference in C80 about conventional microscopy limitations is logical given the anatomy described in C79. This background is crucial for understanding the experimental design.

result: Existing technology only allowed imaging one side of a ganglion at a time, capturing at most half of the neuronal ensemble: at most ~15% of 6000 neurons in Aplysia pedal ganglion and fewer than 50% of 400 neurons in leech segmental ganglion.
evaluation: Claims C18-C21 establish the limitations of previous technology that motivated this work. The specific percentages (C20-C21) provide quantitative context for the improvement achieved. These claims accurately characterize the state of the field before this work and justify the need for the double-sided approach. The limitation is inherent to the anatomy (neurons on both surfaces) rather than technical inadequacy of previous microscopes.

result: Previous VSDs had limitations: electrochromic dyes in sea slugs lacked sufficient sensitivity to detect subthreshold potentials, and FRET-based dyes in leech had non-negligible delay between optical signal and voltage change.
evaluation: Claims C22 and C23 accurately characterize limitations of previous dyes with appropriate citations (Bruno et al., 2015; Hill et al., 2015; Briggman et al., 2005; Briggman and Kristan, 2006). This provides important context for why the VF2.1(OMe).H dye represents an improvement. The claims are factual descriptions of prior work rather than new findings, but are essential for understanding the technical advances in this study.

result: A primary feature of the system is high-speed acquisition without delay between focal planes, which cannot currently be achieved by wide-brain volumetric Ca2+ imaging in C. elegans. VSD recordings containing both spikes and postsynaptic potentials enable inference of network connectivity, offering advantages over techniques accessing only spike events or Ca2+ concentration.
evaluation: Claims C73-C76 highlight key advantages of the system. The comparison to C. elegans imaging (C74) is supported by citations (Schrödel et al., 2013; Kato et al., 2015). The potential for connectivity inference (C75) is a reasonable inference, though noted as beyond the scope of this study. The advantage over other techniques (C76) is a logical conclusion. These claims appropriately position the work relative to other approaches in the field.

result: A single light source was sufficient for illuminating both surfaces because the leech nervous system is sufficiently translucent. Leech ganglionic neuron somata have passive membrane properties with electrotonically attenuated action potentials, showing small spikes in typical interneurons/motor neurons but larger spikes in sensory neurons and some neurosecretory cells. Synaptic interactions during fictive behaviors usually result in compound synaptic potentials detectable in the cell body, enabling a low-noise imaging system with sensitive voltage sensors to record behaviorally-relevant responses even in small neurons.
evaluation: Claims C82-C87, C89-C90 describe important properties of the leech nervous system that make it suitable for VSD imaging. The translucency (C82) is a design advantage. The electrophysiological properties (C83-C87, C89) are established knowledge that explains why somatic VSD imaging can capture behaviorally relevant signals despite signal attenuation. The inference in C90 is well-justified by the combination of system capabilities and neuronal properties. This provides important context for interpreting the results.

result: The double-sided microscope is compatible with intracellular and extracellular electrode placement from at least one side, enabling detailed electrophysiological interrogation alongside optical imaging. VSD traces can be directly compared to intracellular recordings, allowing cell identification by comparison to previously published activity patterns. Optically recorded signals matched typical patterns of fictive behaviors previously characterized by electrophysiology and single-sided VSD imaging.
evaluation: Claims C91, C126-C129 describe important capabilities for validation and cell identification. The compatibility with electrodes (C91, C128) is demonstrated throughout the manuscript with simultaneous recordings. The ability to compare VSD and intracellular recordings (C126-C127) is a key advantage for validation and cell identification. The match to previous characterizations (C129) validates the technique. These capabilities are essential for rigorous neuroscience experiments.

result: Local bending is a withdrawal response to tactile stimulation where the leech bends away from the stimulated location. Fictive local bending can be induced in isolated ganglia by stimulating pressure-sensitive P cells, which causes excitation and inhibition in local bend interneurons (LBIs) that synapse onto motor neurons to produce appropriate contraction/relaxation patterns depending on which P cell was stimulated.
evaluation: Claims C44-C47 provide essential background about local bending behavior with appropriate citations (Kristan et al., 2005; Lockery and Kristan, 1990; Baljon and Wagenaar, 2015). This is well-established knowledge about the leech nervous system that provides context for the experimental design. The circuit organization described is well-documented in the literature. This background is necessary for understanding the local bending experiments.

result: It has long been known that local bending involves population coding, but the exact algorithm and computation remain unknown.
evaluation: Claims C93 and C94 accurately characterize the state of knowledge about local bending with extensive citations (Lewis and Kristan, 1998a-c; Lewis, 1999; Thomson and Kristan, 2006; Kretzberg et al., 2016). This establishes that while the involvement of population coding is known, mechanistic details remain unclear. This provides important context for why comprehensive recording of neuronal populations is valuable. The acknowledgment of what remains unknown is scientifically appropriate.

result: The double-sided microscope technique should be broadly applicable to experimental questions requiring simultaneous imaging from two widely spaced cell layers in Drosophila, sea slugs, and other organisms. An equivalent system could be constructed using alternative parts such as Thorlabs CERNA components.
evaluation: Claims C69, C70, and C72 are speculative statements about potential future applications and alternative implementations. While the speculation is reasonable given the demonstrated capabilities, these claims are not tested in the manuscript. The citations to work in other organisms (Kohsaka et al., 2017; Bruno et al., 2015; Hill et al., 2015) suggest feasibility, but actual implementation would require validation. These are appropriate forward-looking statements but should not be considered established results.

result: To gain more insight into neuronal networks responsible for behavior, more accurate neurocartography will be necessary, achieved by combining functional mapping using machine learning with connectomic approaches using serial block face scanning electron microscopy. This combination with double-sided VSD imaging will enable future investigations of how all neurons in a CNS are recruited to process sensory information and generate distinctive behaviors from overlapping circuits.
evaluation: Claims C116-C118 outline future research directions with appropriate citations (Frady et al., 2016; Pipkin et al., 2016). While these are reasonable and well-motivated plans, they represent proposed future work rather than current results. The combination of techniques described is logical and promising, but the actual insights that will be gained remain to be demonstrated. These are appropriate statements about future directions but should not be evaluated as current findings.

result: Voltage sensors have enabled examination of ethologically relevant neuronal dynamics and functional mapping in sea slugs and medicinal leech. Pan-neuronal Ca2+ imaging can be performed in animals with small neuronal populations including larval zebrafish and C. elegans. Technological advances have enabled brain-wide recording with sufficient resolution to identify individual neurons.
evaluation: Claims C9-C11, C17, and C132-C134 provide background context about prior work in the field with appropriate citations. These accurately characterize the state of neuroimaging technology and establish the context for this work. The claims are factual descriptions of published work rather than new findings, but are essential for understanding how this study fits into the broader field. The citations support each claim.
